canonicalExplanation.summary: An **interface** is a named contract: "anything that is a Notifier has `send(String message)`". Classes **opt in** with `implements Notifier`, and must honour both the signature and the **documented behaviour**. Code that depends on `Notifier` (not `EmailNotifier`) works with **any** implementation, which is exactly what makes testing easy: pass a `MemoryNotifier` that just records messages. Java has **no duck typing**: a class with a matching `send` method but no `implements` clause is **not** a Notifier. Keep interfaces **small and focused**; many tiny ones beat one giant one.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner's OrderService creates an EmailNotifier inside itself, so every unit test tries to send real email and fails offline. They also assume a SmsSender class with a `send(String)` method "counts as" a Notifier. FileNotifier and MemoryNotifier implement one Notifier interface, letting a service test against the memory implementation without branching on concrete types. In this lesson you'll design and use a focused interface with at least two conforming implementations.

examples.title: A Notifier you can test without email
examples.situation: FileNotifier and MemoryNotifier implement one Notifier interface, letting a service test against the memory implementation without branching on concrete types.
walkthrough: **Implement one Notifier interface:** each class declares implements Notifier and defines send.
**Letting a service test against the memory implementation:** new OrderService(memory).place("pen") records [Ordered pen].
**Without branching on concrete types:** OrderService never checks instanceof; a FileNotifier will plug in the same way.
examples.result: Tests run offline and the service works with any notifier.

examples.title: The SmsSender that didn't fit
examples.situation: A learner passes an SmsSender with send(String) to OrderService and gets a compile error.
walkthrough: Java checks declared interfaces, not matching method names.
Add implements Notifier to SmsSender (if it honours the contract),
or wrap it in a small adapter class that implements Notifier.
examples.result: SMS notifications plug into the service deliberately.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Any classes with matching method names already satisfy a Java interface without declaring implements or honoring semantic behavior.
misconceptions.correction: A class is a subtype only when it declares implements, and it must honour the interface's documented behaviour, not just its method names.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why couldn't the class be passed as a Notifier?

analogy.example: An interface is like **a standard plug socket**. Any appliance with the **certified plug** (implements) works in it, whatever's inside. An appliance with a plug that merely looks similar but isn't certified won't be accepted. For testing, you plug in **a meter** (MemoryNotifier) instead of a real kettle.
limitations: Real sockets accept knock-offs; Java doesn't.
A multi-socket with 12 kinds of plug is an oversized interface.

steps.explanation: The service receives an implementation of one Notifier interface.
It calls send without branching on concrete types.
Tests check the memory implementation instead of real email.

nearTransfer.prompt: Design interface PriceSource { long priceCents(String item); } with a FixedPriceSource (map-backed) and use it in a Checkout class. Write a test using a fixed price map.

farTransfer.prompt: Split a large interface (send, retry, schedule, exportCsv) into focused interfaces, update two implementations and two clients so each client depends only on what it uses, and show that a new implementation needs only the small interface.
expectedEvidence: All code compiles and tests pass.

remediation.explanation: For each dependency ask: **does this class need the concrete type, or just a capability?** Depend on a small interface for the capability, and pass implementations in.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The SmsSender that didn't fit".

recap.summary: To design and use a focused interface, declare a small contract with documented behaviour, have classes implement it explicitly, make clients depend on the interface and receive implementations through constructors, and use simple in-memory implementations for testing.
